summary: The first proposal for a file transfer protocol on the ARPANET, written at MIT Project MAC. It argues for indirect use of remote computers, where you move files between systems without logging in to each one and learning its quirks. It was a draft for discussion, later revised in RFC 172.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of walking over to a friend's house to read their book, you ask a helper to copy it and bring it to you. This note describes how that helper should work between computers.

subtitle: The first proposal for a file transfer protocol on the ARPANET, built for indirect use of remote computers.

tldr.problem: Using a remote computer directly means logging in and learning its conventions, while users wanted to move files between very different systems without that.
tldr.mechanism: Cooperating processes on each host exchange transactions made of a 72-bit descriptor and data, using request, response, transfer and terminate types over a single full-duplex NCP connection.
tldr.outcome: It is a first-cut draft for discussion, with passwords and other features left as extensions, and it was updated by RFC 133, 141, 171 and 172.

today: RFC 114 is a draft with status unknown, later updated by RFC 133, RFC 141, RFC 171 and RFC 172.

sections.title: Direct and Indirect Use
sections.content:
The RFC splits network use into two kinds. In direct use you log into a remote host and use it like a local user, so you must know its conventions. In indirect use an intermediate process hides the differences, and you need only a standard set of file transfer commands on your own system.

The protocol was developed for immediate implementation on two MIT hosts, the GE645/Multics and the PDP-10/DM/CG-ITS. It also covers running programs on remote hosts. The author calls it a first cut at a protocol that lets users at any host use the file system of every cooperating host.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either travel to another house and learn its rules, or you can ask a helper who knows the rules to fetch things for you.

sections.title: Transactions and Their Types
sections.content:
The protocol is built from transactions. Each has a 72-bit descriptor holding a 24-bit code, an 8-bit filler count, a NUL, a 24-bit data count and a NUL, followed by data and filler. The first code byte is the transaction type and the second is the data type.

There are four basic types: request, response, transfer and terminate. Requests include Identify, Retrieve, Store, Append, Delete, Rename, Lookup, Open, Close and Execute. A host may implement only a subset and refuse the rest with an unsuccessful terminate. Error codes such as Access denied or File search failed ride in the terminate.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is like a labeled envelope that says what kind of message it is and how much is inside.

sections.title: Sequences, Data Types and Connections
sections.content:
A transaction sequence begins with a request and ends with a terminate. For Retrieve, the server sends rs, then the file, then a successful terminate. For Store, the server sends rr, then the user sends the file. Either host can abort with an unsuccessful terminate, or more drastically with a CLS.

Data type codes describe how to read the data, for example ASCII, EBCDIC, binary and several number formats. Hosts are recommended to accept network ASCII and binary. Cooperating processes listen on a prearranged socket and use one full-duplex connection for both data and control, starting with the connection method of RFC 66 as modified by RFC 80.
sections.plainLanguage: A file trip works like ordering at a counter: you ask, the helper says ready, the thing is handed over, and they say done.

sections.title: Extensions and Access Control
sections.content: The design is meant to be extended with new request types, error codes and data types. Users are identified only by a name sent at the start, and passwords are not suggested at this stage. The author proposes a later password? transaction type, a uniform way to describe file attributes in headings, and a transaction sequence identification number so several requests can share one connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The first version is a simple helper with room to add a password check and other tools later.

references.text: Modification of the initial connection protocol, RFC 80.
